boundary: 'proof' means a written proof in the manuscript, not formal verification; 'exact' means rational or symbolic computation confirming constants and instances; 'numerical' is high-precision floating point; 'exploratory' is an illustration without a claim of generality. Internal AI-assisted review is not peer review or independent reproduction.

claims.statement: C1 costs with c'(z)>0 for z>0: equilibrium link flows are C1 on every open interval with a constant regime, along any C1 demand path, on any network; E is C1, and S and P are C1 when every z c_e(z) is strictly convex (as for BPR costs).
The one-sided extension at t0=0 fails for some costs with zero slope only at zero; whether it fails for BPR costs is open.
For costs a_e + b_e z^p_e with a_e>=0, b_e>0, p_e>1, the slope inequalities of CDS Theorem 4.4(i) hold weakly for E and P at every nested breakpoint of a proportional demand path.
For almost every free-flow vector, every nondegenerate nested breakpoint has a strict slope jump for E and P.
Five-link common-quartic BPR network with a genuine expansion at t=1: E(t)=E0(t)-(84672/78125)(t-1)_+^5+O((t-1)_+^6); E,P in C4 but not C5; E'(1)=164/5.
Three links suffice for E,P in C4 but not C5 with strictly convex polynomial costs, and with mixed BPR exponents at a contraction.
For every p>1 and odd m>=3, m+2 links give E,P in C^(2m-2) but not C^(2m-1).

claims.status: proof; finite enumeration as a check
claims.statement: Five links are minimal for equal-slope nested breakpoints (expansions and contractions) among costs a_e+b_e z^p, a_e,b_e>0, common p>1, all simple paths, proportional positive demands.

claims.status: proof; exact interval check; numerical value
claims.statement: At the optimum-side transition t=1/gamma, S in C^(2m-1) but not C^(2m); the same for P when E is C^(2m) there (checked exactly for the quartic example); the P jump value (about +89.7) is numerical.
After the five-link expansion the connector carries about 0.0088% of A's demand at t=1.1; link flows are C2 but not C3 at the switch.
On the Sioux Falls test network, link activations along a demand scaling are transverse with visible slope drops of about 3.3-3.4%.
